question: What does Python's statistics.pstdev compute?
answer: Python's statistics.pstdev computes the population standard deviation of a data set [S1].

citations.text:
Frequently Asked Questions
Which Python version does the course use? The course uses Python 3.12 in all examples and tests.
Which editor should I use? Any editor is allowed; VS Code is used in the demonstrations.
Is the statistics module allowed in assignments? Yes. statistics.variance(data) returns the sample variance, while statistics.pvariance(data) returns the population variance. In the same way statistics.stdev is the sample standard deviation and statistics.pstdev is the population standard deviation.
Where do I ask questions? Post them on the course forum; answers are usually given within two working days.

S3.title: Python Glossary Overloaded Terms
S3.text: class: in Python a class is a blueprint for creating objects. It is not a category label as in classification problems. function: a reusable block of code defined with def. It is not necessarily a mathematical function. mode: when opening a file the mode string such as "r", "w" or "a" says how the file is used. statistics.mode(data) is a different thing: it returns the most frequent value. sample: random.sample(population, k) draws k unique elements without replacement. It has nothing to do with a statistical sample unless you use it to build one. normal: random.gauss(mu, sigma) and random.normalvariate(mu, sigma) draw numbers from a normal distribution. seed: random.seed(n) makes the random sequence reproducible, so a program prints the same random numbers on every run. iterable: an object you can loop over, such as a list or string.

S4.title: Python Glossary Overloaded Terms
S4.text: program prints the same random numbers on every run. iterable: an object you can loop over, such as a list or string.  An iterator is the object that produces the values one at a time and is returned by iter(iterable). generator: a function that uses yield to produce values lazily, one at a time, instead of building a whole list in memory. decorator: a function that wraps another function; written with the @ syntax above a def line. mean: Python has no built-in mean. Use statistics.mean(data), or statistics.fmean(data) for a faster floating-point mean.

S5.title: Python Lecture Notes
S5.text: 1. Variables and Data Types A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in memory. In Python you create a variable by assignment, for example age = 21. Python is dynamically typed: the type belongs to the value, not to the name, so the same name can later refer to a string. The core built-in types are int (whole numbers), float (decimal numbers), str (text), bool (True or False) and NoneType (the single value None, meaning "no value"). The function type(x) reports the type of x. Conversion functions such as int("42"), float("3.5") and str(10) create new values of another type; int("abc") raises a ValueError. Strings are immutable sequences of characters. Indexing starts at zero, so "python"[0] is "p", and negative indexes count from the end, so "python"[-1] is "n". Slicing "python"[1:4] returns "yth" (start included, stop excluded).
